Flea
flē
n. (a small biting insect; David's own figure for himself when a king was hunting him)
Old English fleah. The Hebrew parosh occurs twice, both times in David's mouth, and both times as a measure of how little he was worth pursuing.

Biblical Definition

David used the word twice, in the two scenes where he had Saul in his power and refused him. In the cave at Engedi, after cutting the skirt of Saul's robe and letting him go, he called after him: “After whom is the king of Israel come out? after whom dost thou pursue? after a dead dog, after a flea” (1Sa 24:14). And in the wilderness of Ziph, after taking the spear from beside Saul's head: “Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the LORD: for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains” (1Sa 26:20). The picture is a king with three thousand chosen men hunting a single insect through the hills. David's point is not merely self-abasement; it is the absurdity of the whole campaign, and the waste of a kingdom's strength on a private jealousy. He is also, in both scenes, refusing to lift his hand against the LORD's anointed — a man with a throne promised him, waiting for God to give it rather than taking it.

Webster 1828 Definition

Webster (1828) defines a flea as an insect of the genus Pulex, remarkable for its agility in leaping, and troublesome by its bite.

expand to see more

FLEA, n. [Sax. flea; from the root of flee, to spring.] An insect of the genus Pulex.

The flea has a compressed body, and is remarkable for its agility in leaping.

After whom dost thou pursue? after a dead dog, after a flea. 1 Sam. xxiv.

FLEA, v.t. To clean from fleas.

Key Scripture

1Sa 24:14 — "After whom is the king of Israel come out? after whom dost thou pursue? after a dead dog, after a flea."

1Sa 26:20 — "Now therefore, let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the LORD: for the king of Israel is come out to seek a flea, as when one doth hunt a partridge in the mountains."

Pro 30:24 — "There be four things which are little upon the earth, but they are exceeding wise:"

Pro 30:27 — "The locusts have no king, yet go they forth all of them by bands;"

Modern Corruption

Self-deprecation is now a social manner rather than a judgment about oneself, while David's flea is a statement made under pressure by a man who could have taken the throne that night.

expand to see more

It is easy to hear after a dead dog, after a flea as the polite modesty of a courtier, and to miss where David was standing when he said it. He had just come out of a cave holding a piece of Saul's robe; in the other scene he was holding Saul's own spear, taken from beside the king's head while the whole camp slept. Abishai had offered to pin Saul to the earth with one stroke and asked no second permission. David's refusal — who can stretch forth his hand against the LORD's anointed, and be guiltless? — is the context of the flea. A man who genuinely holds himself small is not the man who has nothing; he is the man who has the opportunity and does not take it. Modern self-deprecation costs nothing because it is spoken by people with no spear in their hand.

The second thing worth naming is what David refuses to do with a promise. He had been anointed by Samuel years before; the kingdom was pledged to him by God; Saul was demonstrably rejected. Every argument for seizing the moment was available, and Abishai even framed it as providence — God hath delivered thine enemy into thine hand this day. David answers that the LORD shall smite him, or his day shall come to die, or he shall descend into battle and perish; but not by my hand. That is one of the clearest tests in Scripture of the difference between believing a promise and forcing it. Providence supplying an opportunity is not the same as God commanding an act, and a Christian who has learned to tell those two apart has learned something most men never do.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew parosh (H6550), a flea; used only in David's two speeches to Saul; with meshiach YHWH, the LORD's anointed, the reason for his restraint.

expand to see more

Hebrew parosh (H6550) — a flea; after a dead dog, after a flea; 1 Samuel 24:14, 1 Samuel 26:20.

Hebrew keleb meth — a dead dog; the companion figure of worthlessness; 1 Samuel 24:14.

Hebrew mashiach (H4899) — anointed; the title David would not lift his hand against; 1 Samuel 24:6.

Hebrew qore (H7124) — a partridge; the bird hunted in the hills, David's second figure; 1 Samuel 26:20.

Hebrew radaph (H7291) — to pursue; after whom dost thou pursue; 1 Samuel 24:14.

Usage

"“After a dead dog, after a flea” — said with the king's robe in his hand."

"“The king of Israel is come out to seek a flea” — three thousand men after one insect."

"“Let not my blood fall to the earth before the face of the LORD” — an appeal, not a threat."
